say: Pull the trigger on a drill and it feels like one simple thing. It's not. It's six parts working as a team. Let's take it apart, piece by piece.
At the bottom is the battery, a pack of lithium ion cells. Fun fact: the first cordless drill showed up in nineteen sixty one, running on nickel cadmium.
Squeeze the trigger and you close a circuit, so power can flow. Most triggers are variable. The harder you squeeze, the faster it spins.
That power reaches the motor, which spins really fast, thousands of turns a minute. But fast isn't strong. On its own, it would stall on the first big screw.
So next comes a planetary gearbox. A little sun gear in the middle, planet gears around it, all inside a toothed ring. It trades speed for twisting force.
Then the clutch, that numbered ring near the front. Set it low, and once the screw is snug, it slips and clicks, instead of chewing up the screw head.
And at the very front, the chuck. Three jaws close together around the bit and keep it perfectly centered while it spins.
Now put it all back together. Battery, trigger, motor, gears, clutch, chuck. One squeeze, and six parts do their job in a fraction of a second.
